articles.title: This Future Justice Helped Break The Code That Doomed Pearl Harbor’s Architect
articles.content:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day!

On this Veterans Day, consider a future Supreme Court justice who enlisted in the Navy on December 6, 1941 — one day before the attack on Pearl Harbor. He spent the war as a codebreaker in the Pacific, earning a Bronze Star, and his team’s work decrypting Japanese radio traffic helped American pilots locate and shoot down the plane carrying Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, the mastermind of the Pearl Harbor attack. Decades later, he said that targeted killing of a single named enemy had sown his first doubts about the death penalty. Name the justice.

Hint: A Chicago native who finished first in his class at Northwestern law.

See the answer on the next page.

The post This Future Justice Helped Break The Code That Doomed Pearl Harbor’s Architect appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: White House Counsel Goes Full Mob Consigliere, Threatens Dems If They Investigate Trump
articles.content:
On Saturday, the President of the United States announced on Truth Social that Democrats promising to investigate his administration are “SLEAZEBAGS” who “should go to jail,” adding, “I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!” On Sunday, Attorney General Todd Blanche declined to rule out prosecuting members of Congress for the non-crime of scheduling hearings. And thus we add another paragraph to the already lengthy ethical complaint that should permanently strip Blanche of his license to practice law.
But Blanche isn’t the only lawyer playing bumbling mob consigliere these days.
On Monday, White House Counsel Will Scharf wrote to Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of House Oversight, also threatening criminal prosecutions for any Democrat that tries to investigate Trump.
Punchbowl News posted the three-page letter issuing a blanket, preemptive threat to weaponize the DOJ to keep Dems from asking more questions about Trump’s bosom buddy Jeffrey Epstein:
The Supreme Court has held that “[i]nvestigations conducted solely for the personal aggrandizement of the investigators or to ‘punish’ those investigated are indefensible.” Watkins v. United States, 354 U.S. 178, 187 (1957). Congressional investigations must further a legitimate legislative task; Congress cannot employ them to exercise powers of criminal prosecution assigned to the Executive and the Judiciary.
This is true in the abstract. Congress does need a legislative purpose to conduct an investigation. What he glides over is that Congress has massive latitude to define its purpose, every investigation Dems have talked about is clearly within that window, and there’s absolutely no criminal liability even if they weren’t.
I’d say other than that he’s doing fine, except he made other stupid points too.
That Watkins quote is accurate at least. That’s actually a win with Trump’s gaggle of lawyers. But Scharf might have wanted to read the whole case. In Watkins, the Supreme Court held that Congress can’t hold someone in contempt if the questioning isn’t clear enough to put the witness on notice that they might need to invoke their Fifth Amendment rights. That matters for those in Trump’s orbit, but it’s not clear Trump even has Fifth Amendment rights at this point. After Trump v. United States, it’s not exactly clear what of the many scandals Dems hope to investigate wouldn’t enjoy this Supreme Court’s grant of functional immunity.
Watkins did not, however, set limits on the acceptable motives of congressional investigations. And this case was about the RED SCARE, so the Court had every reason to denounce those motives as illegitimate.
Democrats propose investigations into corrupt dealing and conspiracies to circumvent statutory and court ordered limits. Compare these “motives” to the last GOP House. Jim Jordan subpoenaed a former Manhattan prosecutor over a state prosecution of Trump. There was no need for a court to question motives… the explicit reason Jordan provided had no possible federal legislative purpose. Nobody in Trump’s circle wrote three pages about the dignity of the process then.
For what it’s worth, back when Republicans were trying to manufacture a federal reason to interfere in the Manhattan courts, Scharf was on the frontlines rambling incoherently about it.
Scharf does slightly better with Trump v. Mazars, in that the case actually addresses the prospect of an invalid congressional investigation. Unfortunately, the reason that decision came down 7-2 is that it left Alito and Thomas bleating from the outside about the investigation. The majority in that case didn’t reject the investigation outright, but sent it back to the district court to build a record. The district court narrowed the subpoena but otherwise approved some of the rationales for investigation. The matter was settled before working its way back up the appeals process.
Garcia, for his part, has answered Scharf’s letter like someone who has actually read the relevant case law: “Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight … We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats.”
Several Democrats have played fast and loose with the solemnity of congressional probes. When they’re posting “LAWYER UP” on social media as victory-lap posturing, it does a disservice to the gravity of the process. That said, “lawyer up” — the phrase that sent the West Wing to the fainting couch — has been a MAGA staple for years.
In any event, social media bragging doesn’t mean there’s not a clear legislative interest here.
Congress wrote the Impoundment Control Act, which Trump and his DOGE toadies actively assaulted. Congress wrote the immigration laws and funds the agencies carrying them out, and the DOJ and DHS have all but bragged about conspiring to circumvent. Congress is more than free to probe whether it needs to strengthen these laws. It also has the authority to look into impeachment, which should cover all of this stuff.
Which brings us to the part where Scharf graduates from hypocrite to amateur:
Beyond being inconsistent with the clear, well-recognized constitutional limitations on your investigative functions, threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality.
Maybe we should cut Scharf a break because he has personal feelings about legislative investigations. Back when he worked for Missouri’s disgraced governor Eric Greitens, the Missouri House called Scharf as a witness because he’d previously written a memo suggesting Greitens may have obscured donors. Greitens ultimately resigned over the campaign finance scandal anyway. Oh, and Greitens had the felony invasion of privacy and computer tampering issues swirling at the time.
Scharf only works for real winners!
NYU’s Ryan Goodman called the letter “a self-own” that “will very likely damage the Trump administration in any litigation that Congress pursues in courts.” That’s correct. Had Scharf waited for an actual subpoena and argued, in context, that it lacked a legislative hook, that would be lawyering. Firing off this blanket tantrum before the new Congress even gets seated is a clumsy caricature of mob intimidation. Every time the White House objects to an investigation from now on, Congress can hold up this letter as proof that the White House was never even trying to evaluate subpoenas in context.
And then there’s whatever the hell this is:
Bizarrely, you have chalked your motives up to nothing more than “gay” “pettiness” rather than any legislative purpose and compared yourself to a demonic clown.
Scharf is either a guy who thinks The Onion is real or a bigot who thought inserting “gay” into his letter gave it more weight. Why not both?
Garcia quipped that the administration needed to lawyer up. If this is their best lawyering, they might want to consider going pro se.
The post White House Counsel Goes Full Mob Consigliere, Threatens Dems If They Investigate Trump appeared first on Above the Law.

articles.title: When Should Lawyers Stop Networking? 3 Ways To Do Less And Get Better Results.
articles.content:
I open my book, “The Attorney’s Networking Handbook,” with a confession. No one I’ve ever met has wasted more time networking than I have.
Over the years, I’ve attended countless networking events, joined groups, served on boards, and had more coffees, lunches, and cocktails than I care to remember. Some of those experiences were incredibly valuable, while others were a complete waste of time and money.
The good news is that I eventually figured out what works, what doesn’t, and how lawyers can become significantly more effective at networking without making it a second full-time job. Those lessons became the foundation of a book that many attorneys have come to rely on as their guide to networking more successfully.
Here’s something I’ve learned after working with lawyers for nearly two decades. There’s a tipping point in networking that most attorneys never seem to reach.
They’re constantly attending conferences, meeting new people, following up with contacts, and looking for their next opportunity. While there’s nothing inherently wrong with any of that, the problem is that many lawyers continue this cycle indefinitely, never realizing that the ultimate goal should be to network less while generating more business.
I believe that by following three specific strategies, lawyers can potentially reduce their networking time by as much as 80% while improving their results. This isn’t something that happens overnight, but with the right approach, you can build a powerful network that produces business without requiring hundreds of hours of your time every year.
Here’s how to get there.
1. Apply The 80/20 Rule To Your Networking
Most lawyers start networking by spending nearly all their time meeting new people. They attend events, exchange business cards, connect on LinkedIn, and schedule follow-up meetings with anyone who seems remotely interesting.
The problem is that these people are largely unqualified, untested, and essentially strangers. You don’t know whether they have the right relationships, whether they understand your practice, or whether they’re ever going to refer business to you.
This is where the Pareto Principle, commonly known as the 80/20 rule, can change everything.
Your goal should be to identify the relatively small number of relationships that can generate the majority of your referrals. Instead of constantly adding hundreds of new contacts, focus on developing a strategic partner dream team of five to 10 people who know you, trust you, understand your ideal clients, and consistently look for opportunities to help one another.
As these relationships develop, your networking priorities should shift. Ideally, you’ll eventually spend 80% of your relationship-building time strengthening proven partnerships and only 20% meeting new people.
Imagine the difference between chasing hundreds of contacts who barely know you versus investing in 10 strategic relationships with proven friends who are actively looking for opportunities to bring you in on deals.
That’s where networking becomes much more efficient, enjoyable, and profitable.
2. Become A Professional Qualifier Of Your Time
One of the biggest mistakes I see lawyers make is attending networking events without really knowing where to go, why they’re there or who they should be meeting.
Being a professional qualifier of your time means having a clear understanding of your ideal clients and the people who already have relationships with them.
Start by identifying the industries, company sizes, geographic markets, and decision-makers that make up your best potential clients. Then ask yourself who else works with those same people, but in a different capacity.
For example, if you’re an employment lawyer representing midsized businesses, you might develop relationships with HR consultants, commercial real estate lawyers, accountants, or other professionals serving those same companies.
Boutique and specialized law firms can be especially valuable strategic partners because they may work with your ideal clients without directly competing for your area of practice. On the other hand, referring to a full-service firm that already handles employment matters may not be the best use of your relationship-building efforts.
Once you understand who you’re looking for, the next step is figuring out where those people spend their time.
For example, I’m involved with ProVisors, a professional networking organization with approximately 11,000 members, roughly half of whom are attorneys. If you’re a lawyer looking to meet other lawyers who might become referral partners, there’s a pretty good chance you’re going to find some worthwhile relationships there.
The same thinking applies to industry associations, conferences, professional groups, and boards. Rather than attending everything that comes across your desk, focus on organizations where your ideal clients or referral partners are already spending their time.
The objective isn’t to meet as many people as possible. It’s to identify the right people, qualify the relationship, and determine whether there’s a legitimate opportunity to develop a mutually beneficial partnership.
When you become more selective about where you go and who gets your time, you’re much more likely to build that dream team without wasting years on relationships that never go anywhere.
3. Build A Personal Brand That Eventually Does The Networking For You
Of the three strategies, this may be the most important for lawyers who eventually want to spend less time networking and more time practicing law, enjoying their families, or simply having greater control over their schedules.
For years, much of my business came from networking, introductions, and personal relationships. While those activities still matter, I’ve significantly reduced the amount of traditional networking I do because I’ve invested heavily in building my personal brand. Writing for Above the Law is the perfect example. I mean you’re here with me right now working ON your business and learning some new efficiencies.
Through podcasting, writing books and articles, creating useful content, and maintaining a presence on LinkedIn, I’ve been able to develop a level of visibility and credibility that allows people to find me rather than always having to find them. Occasionally, someone will even say to me, “I feel like I’m talking to a celebrity.” While I certainly don’t see myself that way, it’s hard to ignore what that kind of recognition says about the power of building a strong personal brand.
Lawyers can do exactly the same thing.
If you’re a business attorney who becomes well-known for working with manufacturing companies in Chicago, or an estate planning attorney who develops a strong reputation in your local market, you’re going to have a significant advantage over equally capable attorneys whom nobody knows.
This doesn’t mean you need to write five books or host a podcast. It might mean publishing useful LinkedIn content, speaking at industry events, writing articles for trade publications, or becoming a recognizable resource within a particular industry or geographic market.
The key is to start building that visibility now, even if the payoff is several years away.
Think about where you’d like your practice to be in three, five, or 10 years. Would you rather continue attending networking events every week, hoping to find your next client, or become the person people already think of when they need someone with your expertise?
When your relationships and personal brand work together, networking becomes something you choose to do rather than something you feel obligated to do.
The Real Goal Is To Network Less And Generate More Business
I want to be clear that I’m not suggesting lawyers stop networking altogether. Relationships will always be essential to business development, and there will always be value in meeting new people and exploring new opportunities.
What I am suggesting is that networking should become more strategic and less time-consuming as your practice develops.
By applying the 80/20 rule, becoming a professional qualifier of your time, and building a strong personal brand, you can gradually move away from endless networking and toward a more predictable, referral-driven practice.
You may not see an 80% reduction in networking time next year. However, over the next three, five, or 10 years, the difference can be substantial.
The lawyers who understand this aren’t necessarily working harder than everyone else. They’re investing their time in the right relationships, showing up in the right places, and building a reputation that attracts opportunities long after they’ve left the room.
And isn’t that ultimately what we all want? To build a successful book of business without sacrificing every evening, lunch hour, and weekend to get there?
Build your book. Own your future. BE THAT LAWYER.
Steve Fretzin is a five-time bestselling author, host of the BE THAT LAWYER and Future Rainmakers podcasts, and a business development coach who works exclusively with attorneys. For more than 18 years, he has helped lawyers build strong books of business without selling, pitching, or chasing, using his proven Sales-Free Selling™ approach. His clients consistently become top rainmakers and credit his coaching and systems for driving meaningful, measurable growth. articles.title: Why Blue California Voters Rejected Implementing The Nation’s First Wealth Tax
articles.content:
One of the more competitive electoral races in California involved Proposition 40, a referendum that would impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires. Being a reliable blue state in addition to the Democratic sweep of both houses of Congress, it seemed like this measure would pass, and California would have the nation’s first wealth tax.
But days went by without a projection announcement. The no votes had a slight lead, and the yes votes never caught up. Seven days after election day, the major news outlets in California projected that Proposition 40 would not pass.
For many, this is a surprising result. The state’s demographics seem to suggest they would favor a tax on billionaires. So what happened?
A major reason for its failure was that the referendum was not supported by all Democrats in California. The most well known are Gov. Gavin Newsom and Gov.-Elect Xavier Becerra. Democrat-leaning organizations such as the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood also opposed the measure.
They and Republicans feared that the wealth tax would drive away entrepreneurs and the billionaires that already pay significant amounts of income tax. This would hurt the state’s finances in the long term.
The wealth tax also comes at a bad time. Over the past few years, several large businesses have left California due to taxes and regulations. McKesson moved its headquarters from California to Texas in 2019. Charles Schwab relocated from San Francisco to North Texas around 2019-2020. Oracle shifted its headquarters from Silicon Valley to Austin in 2020. Tesla moved its headquarters from Palo Alto to Austin in 2021. Hewlett Packard Enterprise left for Texas around the same period. Chevron, with deep California roots, announced its move from San Ramon to Houston in 2024. SpaceX and X (formerly Twitter) followed to Texas in 2024. More recent departures include Realtor.com’s shift from the Bay Area to Austin in 2025 and John Paul Mitchell Systems’ relocation to Texas that same year. These moves have been repeatedly linked by company leaders to high taxes, heavy regulation, and the overall cost of doing business.
Many, including Democrats, were suspicious of this tax because almost all of the revenue collected would go to the health care industry. The Service Employees International Union (SEIU) who spearheaded this referendum stated that the wealth tax is necessary in order to address federal cuts to health care programs laid out in the One Big Beautiful Bill. Otherwise, many Californians, particularly low-income residents relying on the Medi-Cal program could be forced to go without health insurance. In addition, hospitals could either cut services or close altogether.
Even though Proposition 40 failed, the billionaires should remain on high alert. What is to stop SEIU or a similar organization from reviving the referendum in 2028? The authors of the referendum plan to put the wealth tax back on the ballot again. Or what if special interest organizations banded together and proposed a new wealth tax, this time at 10%? To address this, two competing referendums were also on the ballot that would limit or prohibit a wealth tax in California.
Proposition 41, which did not pass, would have required pre-election audits for ballot initiatives proposing special taxes and would undergo state audits every four years to determine program effectiveness and cost-saving measures. Proposition 42 would prohibit taxes enacted on or after January 1, 2026, on the ownership of individually owned assets. As of the date of publication, there is no decision on whether this referendum has passed or failed although the yes vote has a slight lead at 51.6% of the vote.
Some billionaires have taken action. For example, Meta/Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg considered leaving California due to the wealth tax. But Zuckerberg made an arrangement with Meta where he would stay in California if a new class of nonvoting stock was issued to him which he can then sell to pay the wealth tax. Critics argue that this would dilute the value of Meta shares.
Whether a wealth tax is an appropriate method of generating government revenue is debatable. But Proposition 40 introduced it in a way that did not generate unified support from the ruling Democrats. If it passed, then other groups will do the same thing. Also, while this was supposed to be a one-time tax, the authors can reintroduce it again if the need arises.
While many can emphasize with the SEIU’s interest in making sure Californians get proper health care, they should have taken this up with the state assembly or senate. There they can discuss all options instead of simply throwing money at the problem.
The California billionaires can rest easy knowing that Proposition 40 did not pass. But another billionaire tax could be on the way.
Steven Chung is a tax attorney in Los Angeles, California. He helps people with basic tax planning and resolve tax disputes. He is also sympathetic to people with large student loans. He can be reached via email at stevenchungatl@gmail.com. Or you can connect with him on Twitter (@stevenchung) and connect with him on LinkedIn.
The post Why Blue California Voters Rejected Implementing The Nation’s First Wealth Tax appeared first on Above the Law.
